tldr: To catch a flying ball with a basket mounted on its back, a quadrupedal robot integrates an external camera prediction system with a reinforcement learning policy directly conditioned on both future landing position and remaining time-to-impact, achieving dynamic interception within an ultra-short window of about 1 second.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed system. An external RGB-D camera and a fisheye camera estimate the ball's landing location and time alongside the robot's pose in real time. These spatiotemporal targets are fed directly into the quadruped's reinforcement learning controller to generate the catching motion.
overview:
The agile athleticism shown by a dog effortlessly catching a thrown ball is an extremely high bar for robots. Catching a ball that falls in roughly one second requires synchronizing perception, trajectory prediction, communication, and whole-body locomotion control with ultra-low latency.

Traditional quadrupedal robot locomotion typically relies on a hierarchical design where a high-level planner issues velocity commands (translational and yaw rates) for a low-level policy to track. However, this approach cannot account for strict temporal constraints like "reach the target by a specific deadline," leading to temporal misalignment where the robot arrives too early or too late. Furthermore, aggressively ramping up velocity to arrive in time often triggers degenerate locomotion, causing the robot's torso to sag or pitch excessively.

To solve this, the authors propose a time-constrained reinforcement learning framework that directly feeds the relative target position and remaining time-to-impact into the locomotion policy, bypassing intermediate velocity commands. For the full system, they built an end-to-end pipeline combining two external cameras for real-time tracking, a Kalman filter for predicting landing spot and time, and low-latency communication to the robot's onboard computer.

Through experiments in a physics simulator (MuJoCo) and on hardware (Unitree Go2), the proposed approach achieved higher catching success rates than a velocity-tracking baseline. Furthermore, without explicit instructions, the robot autonomously discovered an efficient "rotate-and-run" behavior, rapidly yawing toward the target before sprinting forward.
contributions: Built a real-time dynamic interception system deployed on hardware, integrating multi-camera visual tracking, parabolic trajectory prediction, low-latency target communication, and reinforcement learning position control.
Proposed a time-constrained reinforcement learning framework that bypasses intermediate velocity commands and directly takes the predicted landing position and remaining time-to-impact as inputs.
Coupled a time-gated reward structure for temporal synchronization with safety terms, preventing degenerate locomotion while naturally eliciting an autonomous rotate-and-run behavior.
Conducted ball-catching experiments in simulation and on a physical Unitree Go2, demonstrating interception success rates significantly higher than a conventional velocity-tracking baseline.

sections.heading: Why is ball-catching so hard for quadrupedal robots?
sections.summary: Intercepting fast-moving objects demands end-to-end agility from perception to motor control. Conventional velocity-tracking and naive position control struggle with timing mismatches and degenerate gaits, necessitating a fresh approach that directly embeds temporal constraints.
sections.details:
Animals like dogs quickly predict the ballistic trajectory of an incoming object and coordinate their entire bodies to catch it with ease. In contrast, replicating this behavior with a quadrupedal robot is not just a matter of running faster. It requires pushing the limits of sensing latency, state estimation jitter, prediction errors, and dynamic whole-body locomotion control all at once.

Most existing reinforcement learning studies for quadrupedal locomotion have focused on velocity tracking, rough terrain traversal, or obstacle avoidance. Very few have directly tackled vision-guided, time-constrained interception. Standard controllers optimize velocity, posture, and energy consumption independently, making it exceptionally difficult to balance all of them within a tight, roughly one-second time window.

Specifically, the authors highlight two major issues: (1) Temporal Misalignment, where the policy focuses solely on minimizing spatial error and fails to arrive at the interception time, and (2) Degenerate Locomotion, where rushing to reach the target causes the torso to collapse or tilt unnaturally.

To overcome these hurdles, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal target-conditioned RL policy that simultaneously receives the landing position and time-to-impact, and evaluates the framework through system-level hardware validation.

sections.heading: Where legged agility and dynamic interception stand today
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work on legged robot reinforcement learning and ball interception. Most existing methods rely on onboard perception or velocity commands, leaving the explicit integration of spatiotemporal conditions into policies for temporal synchronization unexplored.
sections.details:
The authors organize related work into four main perspectives:

- Dynamic Mobility in Legged Locomotion: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have unlocked striking agility, including rough-terrain traversal, high-speed running, and jumping. For object catching, researchers have explored event cameras for ultra-low latency control and robotic arms for grasping. However, these systems do not incorporate explicit time limits into the locomotion policy to synchronize interception timing.

- Position-Conditioned Legged Locomotion: Goal-conditioned policies are widely studied to simplify high-level navigation and skill transitions. Even so, strict temporal synchronization to match exact arrival times and reward designs that prevent degenerate locomotion during aggressive acceleration have not been sufficiently investigated.

- Object Detection and Tracking: Common methods include HSV color thresholding, neural networks like YOLO, and motion capture systems (VICON). Because onboard cameras suffer from motion blur and occlusions during aggressive maneuvers, this work uses two external global cameras overlooking the workspace to ensure reliable robot state estimation and ball tracking.

- Dynamic Trajectory Prediction: Existing approaches include standard Kalman filters (KF), Extended Kalman filters (EKF), and RNN-based acceleration estimators. In this study, the authors adopt a simple Kalman filter modeling gravity for computational efficiency and numerical stability.

sections.heading: System design: Decoupling vision and control while linking space and time
sections.summary: The pipeline predicts the ball's landing point and time using external cameras and a Kalman filter, streaming them directly into an onboard RL policy. Sim-to-real transfer is achieved through teacher-student distillation using privileged information.
sections.details:
The proposed method is broadly divided into a Visual Perception and Trajectory Prediction Pipeline and a Time-Constrained RL Locomotion Policy.

3.1 Visual Perception and Trajectory Prediction Pipeline
To cover the entire workspace, the system uses an RGB-D camera (RealSense D415) placed near the throwing area and a ceiling-mounted fisheye RGB camera. The fisheye camera tracks an AprilTag on the robot's back to estimate its pose $\bm{p}_r^t$. Meanwhile, the D415 camera runs a lightweight YOLOv13n object detector (assisted by parallel HSV thresholding) to detect the ball with sub-10ms latency. A finite state machine (FSM) monitors the ball's vertical velocity and displacement to reliably trigger a "throw event" without false alarms. A Kalman filter (KF) based on a parabolic flight model then estimates the 3D position and velocity to predict the landing spot $\bm{p}_t^t$ and landing time $t_t$. These targets are streamed to the robot's Jetson Orin Nano via LCM communication.

3.2 Time-Constrained Goal-Conditioned RL for Dynamic Interception
Locomotion involving aggressive acceleration, deceleration, and turning is highly sensitive to the sim-to-real gap, such as ground friction and individual motor variations. To address this, a Teacher policy is trained with PPO in simulation using privileged information (such as ground friction and external contact forces). A deployable Student policy is then trained via supervised learning (distillation) to reconstruct these features purely from observable proprioceptive history.

The observation space directly includes the relative goal position error $\Delta\bm{p}^t$, heading error, and normalized remaining time $t_t$. The reward design introduces a time-gated structure that heavily penalizes spatial tracking error only when the remaining time $t_{go}$ drops below a threshold. This discourages the robot from simply rushing ahead or creeping forward slowly, nudging it to arrive right on time. In addition, curriculum learning gradually widens the target distance sampling range (up to 7.5 m), and Random Network Distillation (RND) assists exploration.

captions.F2: Training framework for the local navigation policy. An RL Teacher policy trained with privileged information (friction coefficients, contact forces, etc.) is distilled into a Student policy that relies solely on accessible proprioceptive history, ensuring reliable sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Sim and real tests: Rotate-and-run unlocks superior agility
sections.summary: The authors evaluated the method against baselines in MuJoCo simulations and on a real Unitree Go2. The proposed policy autonomously learned to face the goal before sprinting, achieving precise temporal synchronization and high catch success rates.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a Unitree Go2 equipped with a $22\times 28\times 9\text{ cm}^3$ basket on its back (tolerance margin within 17.8 cm). For comparison, the authors prepared a conventional velocity-tracking baseline guided by a P-controller, as well as an Instantaneous Ball State (IBS) baseline that directly receives the ball's current position and velocity at each frame instead of future landing predictions.

4.2 Simulation Evaluation (MuJoCo)
Across 300 throws landing within 2 meters with flight times between 1.15 and 1.35 seconds, the proposed method consistently achieved high success rates across short and long distances. The IBS baseline failed almost entirely because it could not implicitly learn ballistic prediction inside the policy. Evaluating the Time Ratio (actual arrival time / predicted landing time) showed that the proposed method maintained values below 1.0 at short distances (under 1 m), confirming that the robot reached the landing zone ahead of time and waited steadily.

Locomotion patterns revealed a notable difference. The velocity-tracking baseline relied heavily on lateral sidestepping with low yaw rates. In contrast, without any explicit programmatic rules, the proposed method autonomously adopted a rotate-and-run strategy: quickly yawing toward the target first, then sprinting forward in a straight line. Because forward sprinting is far faster than lateral crab-walking over longer distances, this emerged as an optimal behavior.

4.3 Hardware Verification
In physical trials, 100 throws were tested across distances of 0 to 2 meters with flight times of 0.8 to 1.2 seconds. For Track Success Rate (counting balls that made contact with the basket rim), the proposed method exceeded 60% across all distance ranges. In Catch Success Rate (balls settling securely inside the basket), the margin was even more dramatic. The baseline fell below 10% at short to medium ranges and managed only 25% at long range, rendering it virtually ineffective, whereas the proposed method sustained strong interception performance. The maximum successful interception distance reached 1.70 m for the proposed approach versus 1.23 m for the baseline, demonstrating its real-world robustness.

captions.F6: Time Ratio (actual arrival time / predicted landing time) plotted against interception distance. A ratio below 1.0 indicates arriving ahead of schedule. The proposed method (blue) reliably stays below 1.0 at short distances (under 1 m) and consistently reaches the target faster than the baseline (red) across longer ranges.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: Toward fully autonomous real-world catching
sections.summary: By directly conditioning reinforcement learning on position and time, dynamic ball-catching by a quadruped was demonstrated on hardware. Future work aims to transition to onboard vision, tackle rough terrain, and further boost real-world success rates.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated on real hardware that a quadrupedal robot can intercept a flying ball under strict, roughly one-second time limits by cleanly coupling a perception-prediction pipeline with an RL locomotion policy. Combining a physics-based Kalman filter with a policy directly driven by spatiotemporal targets significantly reduced the sim-to-real gap and produced agile rotate-and-run locomotion.

Nevertheless, the authors candidly discuss current limitations. While hardware catch success rates comfortably outperformed the baseline, room for improvement remains overall. Cumulative errors arise from actuator response latency, visual tracking jitter, and yaw friction on soft surfaces.

Currently, experiments are confined to flat indoor setups within the field of view of external cameras (roughly a 2-meter radius). Furthermore, detailed ablation studies dissecting how much individual components—such as time conditioning, distillation, and specific reward terms—contribute to success rates remain for future work. Moving forward, the team plans to eliminate external cameras by migrating to onboard perception and extend dynamic interception to uneven, rough terrain.

takeaways: In dynamically demanding tasks with tight deadlines, directly feeding target positions and remaining time into the policy is far more effective than traditional hierarchical control with intermediate velocity commands.

Decoupling perception and control—using a classical physical model like a Kalman filter to extrapolate trajectories and feeding them into RL with minimal latency—offers a practical way to prevent sim-to-real failures.
When aggressive acceleration and deceleration are required, RL autonomously discovers that rapidly pivoting in place and sprinting straight is faster than omnidirectional lateral crab-walking.
limitations: Robot localization and ball tracking rely on two external cameras, preventing immediate deployment outside the cameras' field of view or in uninstrumented environments.
Catch success rates on hardware still leave clear room for improvement, impacted by communication delays, actuator latency, and floor resistance on soft surfaces like carpets.
Detailed ablation studies isolating the specific performance contributions of time conditioning, teacher-student distillation, and RND have not yet been conducted.
